newsitem.title: USA: China MFN gaining support in U.S. House.
newsitem.headline: China MFN gaining support in U.S. House.

text.p: Support for President Bill Clinton's decision to maintain normal trade relations with China appears to growing among lawmakers as the House of Representatives prepares to vote on the issue next week.
"It is looking increasingly positive," said Stuart Eizenstat, undersecretary of state for economic affairs.

In recent days a number of conservative and Christian leaders have come forward to voice support for continuing China's Most Favored Nation (MFN) trade status despite their condemnations of human rights abuses.

Their statements of support plus a letter backing China MFN this week from evangelist Billy Graham helped counter arguments by other religious and social conservatives who want to end normal trade relations with China.
"I am in favor of doing all we can to strengthen our relationship with China and its people," Graham wrote in a letter to Rep. David Dreier, a California Republican.

"China is rapidly becoming one of the dominant economic and political powers in the world, and I believe it is far better for us to keep China as a friend than to treat it as an adversary. Furthermore, in my experience, nations respond to friendship just as much as people do," Graham added.
Graham's letter helped shore up support among conservative Republicans worried about religious repression in China.
"Billy Graham's letter has had an electrifying effect," Eizenstat said.

The full House was scheduled to vote on Tuesday on a measure that would disapprove Clinton's decision to renew MFN for another year. Most favored nation trade status is given almost every country in the world. Only a handful are denied MFN status. Without it tariffs on goods imported from China would soar to the high levels of the 1930's.
House Republican Leader Dick Armey announced on Thursday that he would reluctantly support Clinton's MFN decision.

Armey, like other lawmakers, had been reconsidering support for normal U.S. trade ties with China because of reports of human rights abuses, nuclear technology and missile sales and allegations that Beijing tried to influence U.S. elections through illegal campaign contributions.
But in a speech at Johns Hopkins University he said he decided to back MFN status for China and push for other legislation to address concerns about Beijing.

"In my heart, I would like to oppose most favored nation status for China as a way of expressing the deep repugnance I feel toward the tyranny of Beijing," the Texas Republican said. "But intellectually, I believe that continued normal trade relations are best for the people of China today and offer the best prospect for liberating them in years to come."
The influential House Ways and Means Committee voted on Wednesday 34-5 to back Clinton's decision to maintain normal U.S. trade relations with China.
Clinton lobbied hard for China MFN renewal and on Thursday agreed to step up U.S. radio broadcasts to China, a move suggested by Armey, House Speaker Newt Gingrich and others.
Clinton made the announcement in a letter to Gingrich, which was released in Denver where the president was host to the summit of the world's leading industrial nations.

Meanwhile a package of legislative actions on China was being prepared by Dreier and Rep. John Porter, an Illinois Republican. The package would increase financing for the National Endowment for Democracy to fund election monitoring in China. It would also provide more money to for student exchange programs to bring more Chinese students to the United States to study, a congressional aide said.

The legislation also would require the government to maintain a list of Chinese political prisoners and publish a list of companies that do business with Chinese military affiliates. It also would deny visas to Chinese officials involved in human rights abuses and engaged in selling high tech weapons, the aide said.
